paper_title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The bitter lesson predicts that general methods which scale with computation ultimately outperform approaches built around human domain knowledge (Sutton, 2019). However, while progress in informal mathematics has come from scaling frontier models chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025), progress in formal proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around those models. Indeed, formal proof assistants such as Lean (Moura & Ullrich, 2021) express mathematical statements and proofs in precise language that can be checked mechanically. This includes intermediate proof steps, which naturally supports structured search that can be encoded as part of workflow in harness: the tools, context, and control loop around model. Recent formal proving harnesses exploit this structure by orchestrating specialized provers or prescribing planning, decomposition, and proof refinement (Varambally et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Isenbaev & Hanin, 2026; Math Inc., 2026b). Only very recently has interest grown in simple loops that use the harness only to provide Lean feedback and sustain work (Requena et al., 2026; Tsoukalas et al., 2026; Humanfia, 2026; Kabra et al., 2026). Formal mathematics thus raises bitter-lesson question for harness design: with frontier models already capable of reasoning and agentic test-time scaling, can simple test-time scaling loop match specialized workflows? And what should simple harness provide to make that scaling effective and efficient? Do these simple methods offer better performance for the same cost? These questions matter increasingly as frontier models generate research mathematics whose informal arguments are difficult to verify. Indeed, scaling automated theorem proving (ATP) to produce mechanically checked proofs has become necessary component of automated discovery (Tsoukalas et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026b,a; Patel et al., 2026). Yet new workflows are often presented alongside stronger models and more compute, or compared to baselines that scale poorly. This leaves unclear whether their gains hold against an efficient simple loop given enough test-time compute. We tackle these questions with h1, simple harness with an efficient interface to Lean 4 that imposes no decomposition or search structure. This loop keeps model working until success or cost cap stops it by iterating between multi-turn block of reasoning and tool-calling, submission to formal validator, and reflection that compacts the transcript into new context for the next iteration. Each additional iteration is akin to appending Wait to models thinking in s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025), extending the computation available at test time. We evaluate costsuccess curves across benchmarks and open problems, accounting for inference cost and matching models where possible. Our findings are threefold: bitter lesson for specialized harnesses: simple test-time scaling reaches frontier results without prescribed workflows (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). simple loop often matches or Pareto-dominates specialized systems at matched models and comparable budgets, while reaching state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), FATE-X (Jiang et al., 2026), and FormalConjectures100-Solved (Firsching et al., 2026) and settling eight open Formal Conjectures problems, and variants of Erdős 138 (Bloom, 2026a) and 337 (Bloom, 2026b). At matched models, h1 surpasses Goedel-Architect (Chung et al., 2026) at lower estimated cost; on five open Erdős problems, it Pareto-dominates full AlphaProof Nexus (APN) (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) with the same LLM. Longer attempts can be more efficient than repetition (Section 3.3). With sequential test-time scaling, pass@1 traces budget-dependent curve that can Pareto-dominate pass@k: on five Erdős problems, extending h1 can cost less than repeating h1 or APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). simple harness still needs efficient interaction, reliable feedback, and sustained progress (Section 4). Among simple loops, harness design produces large differences in solve rates and cost. Controlled ablations and comparisons with AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026b), and Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026) show the value of reliable and efficient interface to Lean with search tools, loop that sustains repair and reflection, and efficient reasoning and cache reuse. Our results show that simple harness can match or outperform more complex systems, extending the bitter lesson to harness design in ATP and plausibly other structured environments. Frontier models keep improving their reasoning and adaptation to execution feedback, and harnesses should help these capabilities scale through efficient interaction with the environment rather than impose workflows. Future work should thus evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, or risk bitter lesson.

sections.title: 2 Methods
sections.content: We first introduce the formal-proving task, benchmarks, and baselines, and explain how we evaluate test-time scaling. We then describe h1s tools and interaction loop, which let the model work efficiently and sustain progress as its inference budget grows.

sections.title: 2.1 Experimental setup
sections.content: In Lean (Moura & Ullrich, 2021), formal statement specifies mathematical claim and its Formal proving. assumptions; the agent must complete its proof in source file. Mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020) is shared library of formalized mathematics that provides definitions and previously proved results. Compiling the file checks the proof and returns errors. During proof development, open goals list what remains to be proved. Additionally, formal validation tools such as SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024) allow checking the final proof against the original statement, rejecting placeholders for unfinished steps and added assumptions. Benchmarks. We evaluate on formal statements of increasing difficulty. PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024) contains 672 problems from the past Putnam undergraduate competitions; for controlled comparisons, we use Putnam100, the same 100-problem subset used by AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026). We also use the 12 problems of the 2025 Putnam competition, formalized both in PutnamBench and by Numina (Liu et al., 2026b). IMO 2026 contains the 6 problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, the leading competition for high-school students, as formalized by Axiom (Axiom Math, 2026a). FATE-X (Jiang et al., 2026) contains 100 algebra problems at PhD qualifying-exam level or beyond, and FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a) 23 theorems at PhD qualifying-exam level. Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026) collects formalized research conjectures; we evaluate on FC100-solved, random sample of 100 problems with known informal solutions, and on open targets. Appendix C.1 records benchmark source revisions and Lean/Mathlib versions. We omit older benchmarks such as miniF2F (Zheng et al., 2022), which modern models essentially saturate. PutnamBench mainly tests efficiency, while FATE-X, FormalQualBench, and FC100-solved remain unsaturated at our scale. Putnam 2025 and IMO 2026 are recent enough to be unseen by the models released before them (Appendix E.10). Open conjectures, such as those in Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026), test progress beyond problems with known solutions. Models and baselines. We evaluate frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, alongside openweight DeepSeek V4 Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) and Leanstral 1.5 (Kabra et al., 2026). We select baselines representing the most competitive results on our benchmarks as of August 27, 2026, alongside simple loops that help isolate the contribution of harness design. All state-of-the-art (SOTA) claims use this comparison cutoff (Appendix C.2). To compare with human-designed workflows, we include systems that enforce planning, decomposition, or agent roles in code: Goedel-Architect (Chung et al., 2026), MerLean (Li et al., 2026a), and full AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) instead prescribes planreview workflow to general coding agent through instruction files (skills), while Numina (Liu et al., 2026b) gives general coding agent optional tools that consult natural-language (informal) prover and other models, and prescribes subagent workflow for its hardest problem. Comparisons with other simple loops test interaction efficiency and persistence; these include Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026), APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) (AlphaProof Nexuss single-agent loop), and our same-model reruns of both AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) and Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026b). We also report the published scores of trained provers, such as Seed-Prover 1.5 (Chen et al., 2025a), where they still define the SOTA. Appendix discusses additional related work. Measuring test-time scaling with cost per task. Prior work very rarely compares systems at matched inference compute. Earlier theorem-proving work focused on training better models, with evaluation emphasizing solve rates rather than inference cost. As improvements increasingly come from inference-time search, repair, and orchestration, these reporting conventions have persisted even as an attempt has come to mean very different amounts of computation. For example, on PutnamBench, one Goedel-Architect attempt permits up to 16 revisions of its proof plan (Chung et al., 2026), while one AxProverBase attempt permits 50 agent iterations (Requena et al., 2026). Average cost includes all problems, including failures, with each problems cost capped at $B. 2.2 h1: simple harness for efficient test-time scaling h1 keeps model working on Lean proof until an external validator accepts it or the budget runs out (Figure 2). In each iteration, the model reasons and calls tools in ReAct loop (Yao et al., 2023) for at most turns, editing persistent working file; every edit is compiled and returns errors and open goals. The iteration ends when the model submits the file, which an external validator then checks against the original statement, also accepting checked disproofs where supported (Appendix C.2). If the validator rejects the submission, reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback into verified progress, lessons from failed attempts, and useful lemma names, and discourages giving up, as in Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), and AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026); the model then continues from the current file with this summary. The loop builds on APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026), AxProverBase, and the Ralph loop from software engineering (Huntley, 2025; Macedo, 2026). simple loop with an efficient interface. h1 imposes no decomposition, planning, or search structure. Instead, it gives the model an efficient interface to Lean, with targeted edits rather than rewritten proofs, immediate compiler feedback, and context that grows and is cached within an iteration. Optional tools let the model search Mathlib, inspect definitions, and test proof fragments, and the model decides which to use and how to develop the proof. Section 4 shows that these choices matter for both cost and success, and Appendix details tools and prompts.

sections.title: 3 Simple test-time scaling delivers frontier results
sections.content: We first show that frontier models in h1 reach state-of-the-art results across competition and research mathematics. We then show that simple scaling often matches or outperforms specialized workflows at matched models and comparable inference costs, and that, even on open research problems, extending single attempt can be more efficient than repetition. 4 Figure 3 Generalist models reach frontier results through simple scaling. On FC100-solved (left) and FATE-X (right), increasing h1s inference budget takes generalist models beyond published benchmark scores. On FC100-solved, h1 with Gemini 3.1 Pro matches the DeepMind (DM) prover agents score at quarter of its budget cap; with GPT-5.6 Sol, it solves 78, and 90 on FATE-X. With DeepSeek V4 Flash, h1 surpasses AlphaProof on FC100-solved and Leanstral 1.5 on FATE-X. Baseline markers show the best published results as of August 27, 2026.

sections.content: Solving open problems and exposing misformalizations. Beyond the solved subset of Formal Conjectures and benchmarks with possibly known informal solutions, we ran our system on 236 targets selected as open from Formal Conjectures (Appendix D). It settled eight of them  (Table 1)  : variants of Erdős 138 and 337, three OEIS conjectures (A108081, A211417, A022030), the existence of an AME(9, 10) state (Open Quantum Problem 35), and two conjectures of Written on the Wall II. We document concisely the newly proven theorems in Appendix D, and our pull-request marking these as solved2. Equally important as finding these proofs was our systems ability to find misformalizations in Formal Conjectures: formal statements that do not express the intended conjecture. Our system found several by producing short disproofs of the written statement, for instance for the Poincaré conjecture, whose formalization was missing hypothesis. Appendix D.2 lists all misformalizations found, most of which have since been fixed upstream. sections.title: 3.2 The bitter lesson for specialized workflows
sections.content: We show that, at matched models, simple test-time scaling recovers much of the performance of specialized workflows, often at lower inference cost, and that repetition (pass@k) or newer frontier model in the same loop usually closes any remaining gap (Figure 1; Table 2). Simple test-time scaling can match specialized systems at lower cost. On PutnamBench, one extended h1 attempt surpasses Goedel-Architects blueprint-based search, which assigns separate agents to prove the lemmas in dependency graph. With the same DeepSeek V4 Flash model, h1 first matches its pass@1 score at comparable cost, then reaches 598 solves against 597 at pass@4 with informal proof seeding, at an estimated $1.08 versus $1.47 per problem (Chung et al., 2026) (Figure 1, left). Goedel-Architects tool-integrated reasoning baseline reaches only 54.5% at pass@32 on 200-problem subset, compared with h1s 89.0% at pass@1 on the full benchmark with the same model. With Gemini 3.1 Pro alone, h1 also matches Goedel-Architects July leaderboard result of 642 solves, which pairs Gemini 3.1 Pro with the cheaper DeepSeek V4 Pro, at similar cost ($6.32 versus $5.80 per problem). The much stronger performance of simple harness with the same model illustrates how weak simple baseline can overstate the need for specialized workflows (Figure 7). simple loop solves the problem that needed hand-designed workflow. single model in h1 also recovers the result of Numina-Lean-Agent, which reserved specialized workflow for the hardest problem of Putnam 2025. Numina runs Opus 4.5 in Claude Code, general coding agent, with optional tools that call other models: an informal prover built as Gemini 3 Pro generatorverifier loop, and discussion partner (Liu et al., 2026b). For that problem, A5, the authors switch to coordinator that delegates blueprint decomposition, sketching, and proving to subagents, seeded with GPT-5.2 hint and $1,000 budget. On the same statements, GPT-5.2 alone solves all twelve in h1, including A5, in single run per problem and without such workflow, spending $81.52 on A5 against Numinas $1,000 budget  (Table 2)  . Also note that with Opus 4.5 alone, h1 solves seven problems against four for Numina without its informal prover, consistent with our finding that Claude Code, on which Numina builds, scales less effectively than h1 with the same model (Section 4). Repetition closes most remaining gaps. When single h1 run falls short, rerunning the unsolved problems from fresh context (residual pass@k) closes most remaining gaps. Like h1 itself, repetition prescribes no workflow; it simply adds independent attempts, though often at higher cost than extending single run (Section 3.3). As long as that cost is counted, including failed attempts, repetition therefore belongs to the simple baseline against which specialized workflows should be tested. On Putnam 2025, h1 with Opus 4.7 solves eleven against MerLeans twelve; retrying the remaining problem recovers all twelve within six attempts. On full PutnamBench, extra attempts on the last two problems let h1 with GPT-5.5 match Aleph Provers (Logical Intelligence, 2026) final 672/672 coverage at an estimated $17.86 versus about $74 per problem, counting the cost of failed attempts (Appendix C.4). On FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a), OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) instructs Claude Code to cycle through planning, proving, review, and replanning, generating several candidate proofs per open goal and extracting helper lemmas when goal is stuck. The best of four h1 runs with Opus 4.6 matches its eight solves under the same four-hour limit. sections.title: 3.3 Persisting can beat repetition, even on open problems
sections.content: When an attempt can keep going, pass@1 is no longer single number but curve that grows with budget: within one run, the model can abandon an approach and try another. The question becomes whether spending more on one attempt beats spending the same on several. AlphaProof Nexus (APN) (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) found that its basic agent, simple loop like h1, can Pareto-dominate its full system, which evolves proof sketches with LLM raters, parallel provers, and AlphaProof, but only through repetition: at pass@k for large enough k. APN reports each pass@k, including pass@1, as single point at fixed budget, leaving open whether single attempt given more budget can do what repetition does. We evaluate h1 on the six open Erdős problems that APN reports individually, using the same model, Gemini 3.1 Pro. Following APN, we report mean cost conditional on success, charging each group its members summed cost up to the first accepted proof. This metric is undefined for problem with no successful attempts, so Figure 1 (middle) compares the five problems that all three systems solve at least once. For h1, we show how pass@1 changes as the budget grows, rather than reporting single point. As the budget grows, it matches APN basics pass@1 at lower cost, then exceeds both APN basics pass@3 (75.4% at $191) and full APN (76% at $317), reaching 82.5% at $121. On these five problems, giving one h1 attempt more time achieves higher solve rate at lower cost than three attempts of APN basic. Full APN retains an advantage 7 Figure 4 (Left) Detailed prompts sustain progress on open problems. With Gemini 3.1 Pro on six open Erdős problems and $150 cap per attempt, single attempt with detailed prover and reflection prompts, which among other things deflect giving up and cheating, outperforms six attempts with brief ones. (Right) Moderate numbers of turns between reflections outperform both extremes. Solves with Gemini 3 Flash on Putnam100 ($20 cap) and Gemini 3.1 Pro on FATE-X ($50 cap) as the number of turns between reflections varies. over both APN basic and h1 on the remaining problem, Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts (Appendix E.6). APNs conditional metric gives first view of this depthbreadth trade-off, but omits spending on groups with no accepted proof (Appendix E.6). To account for these costs and separate compute allocation and isolate differences between harnesses, we also compare longer attempts with repetition within h1, using mean spend across all successful and failed groups (Figure 13). On the same five problems, pass@1 reaches 82.5% at $138 in mean spend including failures, whereas pass@3 needs $202 to reach at least that rate. Thus, the advantage of longer attempts at these budgets persists when failed searches are charged. Repetition reaches higher success rates at larger budgets. The right balance between depth (longer attempts) and breadth (more attempts) therefore depends on the budget and problem and is hard to set in advance. The bitter lesson suggests leaving this choice to the model rather than to hand-set budgets.

sections.title: 4 What a harness must provide for efficient test-time scaling
sections.content: Leaving the proof workflow to the model does not make the harness irrelevant: with the same model, simple loops differ several-fold in solve rate and cost. We explain these differences, and what makes h1 state-of-theart harness and an effective Lean baseline, by pairing comparisons with other simple loops with ablations on h1 that vary its tools, prompts, reflection, turns between reflections, and reasoning effort. The resulting lessons concern the interface, persistence, and context management, and should transfer beyond the automated theorem proving domain, to agents that work against verifier in rich environments allowing structured development and retrieval, such as software verification and coding in large libraries and codebases. In h1, the model edits An efficient, reliable interface lets the model act in small steps and look things up. persistent working file over many turns, sees compiler feedback after every edit, and can search the library or test proof fragment at any point. AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) instead makes one round of tool calls, then regenerates complete proof after each round of feedback. With the same Gemini 3 Flash model and $20 budget, it solves 18 Putnam100 problems against h1s 69, and trails in all six settings we compare (Figure 5, left). reliable interface also removes avoidable failures by construction: 42.2% of AxProverBases failed compilations stop at an invalid library import, which cannot occur in h1 because its file already imports all of Mathlib (Figure 20). Likewise, h1 retries transient API failures and restores the file after Lean timeout, whereas some Claude Code runs failed through API errors and repeated timeouts even after restarts (Appendix E.9). Library search, which AxProverBase found the least useful of its components, matters much more when the model can act on its results over many turns: without search tools, the REPL, or the language server, h1 solves 49 Putnam100 and 49 FATE-X problems, against 69 and 63 with all tools (Figure 22). Any 8 Figure 5 (Left) h1 Pareto-dominates AxProverBase on Putnam100. For each of six model settings, the arrow goes from AxProverBase to h1, labelled with the gain in solves at comparable or lower budget cap. (Right) Claude Code improves with our Lean tools but still falls short of h1 on FATE-X. With Opus 4.8, replacing Claude Codes built-in shell and file tools with our prompt and Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) raises its solves from 63 to 73, while h1, which also enforces validation, repair, and reflection, reaches 83 (Putnam100: Figure 6). single search tool or the REPL recovers most of this gain, and removing any one tool from the full set costs at most four solves: what matters is the ability to look up and check, not particular tool. Other simple loops with less efficient interfaces reach h1s solve rates only at higher cost. APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) lacks dedicated search tools; on the five-problem Erdős subset, extending single h1 attempt can be more efficient than repeating APN basic (Section 3.3). Humanfia (Humanfia, 2026) checks proofs only through shell commands and restarts its coding agent in fresh session each round, carrying over only the proof file and reviewer feedback; with GPT-5.5, it spends five times more than h1 for the same 670 PutnamBench solves. harness should thus support the model by offering persistent workspace edited in small steps, immediate feedback, ways to retrieve and check what the model needs, and robust handling of predictable failures, leaving their use to the model. The loop, not the model, decides when to stop. Test-time compute helps only if the harness turns larger budget into continued work. With Opus 4.8, native Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026b) solves 63 FATE-X problems; giving it our prompt and our Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), in place of its built-in shell and file tools, raises this to 73, while h1 reaches 83 (Figure 5, right; 81, 95, and 99 on Putnam100). Access to verification helps, but the model can still stop without calling the validator or give up after rejection; in h1, rejection starts another iteration with the working file, the feedback, and reflection summary (Appendix E.9). Within h1, the system prompts matter most on open problems. Unlike one-line prompts, our detailed prompts describe the tools, set rules for statement integrity and disproofs, and tell the prover not to give up because problem is open and the reflection LLM not to endorse such decision (Appendix B.2). On six Erdős problems, single attempt with them outperforms six attempts with one-line prompts at the same $150 cap per attempt (Figure 4, left). Reflection, which carries verified progress and lessons into the next iteration, raises h1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash from 554 to 598 PutnamBench solves, consistent with AxProverBases findings (Figure 7). None of these tells the model how to prove: the harness decides whether the model keeps going, not how. Reuse context, reset it before it degrades, and think more per turn. Each turn in continuing context rereads it from cache, typically ten times cheaper than uncached input and hundred times cheaper than output, whereas each restart discards it. AxProverBase sits at one extreme: output accounts for 89% of its $17.39 per problem, against 34% of h1s $9.00, and it reuses at most 0.5% of its input from cache, against 7494% for h1 (Figure 18). Varying the number of turns between reflections in h1 exposes the same trade-off (Figure 4, right). With one turn, h1 solves 50 Putnam100 and 39 FATE-X problems, against 72 and 65 with ten turns, and pays roughly twice as much per solve. With 200 turns instead of one, the cached share of input rises from 0.2% to 86%, yet solves drop to 60 and 52 (Figure 29): caching makes long contexts cheap but not productive, consistent with context rot (Hong et al., 2025). Thinking more per turn is better use of budget. AxProverBase found that raising the thinking budget from 10k to 32k tokens gains as much as doubling 9 the number of iterations, at lower cost. In h1, higher reasoning effort solves more at lower total cost: with Gemini 3.1 Pro, it solves 89 Putnam100 problems at $20.63 each with low effort and 99 at $5.34 with high effort, needing far fewer compilations (Figure 28). In short, harness for long-horizon agents should let the model work in one context long enough to reuse it, compact that context before it degrades, and favor reasoning over repeated failed attempts.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion, limitations, and discussion
sections.content: Conclusion. We asked whether harnesses for frontier models should prescribe hand-designed workflows or give the model simple loop and larger budget. With h1, simple loop with an efficient interface to Lean, test-time compute alone reaches state-of-the-art results and matches or surpasses hand-designed workflows at the same model and comparable cost. We find that single longer attempt in this loop can even outperform repetition on open problems. Getting the details of the harness right still matters: its interface, persistence, and context management determine how efficiently compute turns into progress. Before designing workflow, one should thus carefully try frontier model in simple loop at realistic budget. Limitations and discussion. We acknowledge that most frontier models are black boxes, and that we cannot measure the extent to which benchmark exposure during training could narrow the gap between specialized workflows and simple loop, but where possible we used models that predate the problems or their solutions, such as Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.2 for Putnam 2025 and GPT-5.6 Sol for IMO 2026 (Appendix E.10). Across the 707 benchmark problems on which we compare the simple loop with specialized workflow, we find only two exceptions where the specialized harness is able to solve problem we are not3. Regarding scale, h1 works on single file, whereas formalizations that exceed context window, such as those of Fermats Last Theorem (Anthropic, 2026a) or entire textbooks (Rammal et al., 2026), require dependency management across files, and codebase-level validation, as well as parallel agents that share intermediate results to complete the task in reasonable time: in OpenAIs NavierStokes resolution, about 10,000 agents exchanged millions of messages over 88 hours (OpenAI, 2026a). Our tools also cover only Lean, not numerical computation, simulation, visualization, or web search. What makes simple loop efficient and effective at that scale is the natural next question. Following the bitter lesson, parallel agents, codebase management, and richer tools should be added without prescribing their use, for instance by letting agents communicate freely rather than through fixed hierarchy. h1s interface and tools are themselves hand-designed, which the bitter lesson might discourage. Yet human design and leveraging computation need not run counter to each other (Sutton, 2019); the question is where each helps most first. In formal mathematics, spending compute on the reasoning of frontier models, and using human effort on the interface currently works best. Further ahead, model could build and deploy its own harness for problem and become more efficient than the human-designed interfaces. 3Full APN solves Erdős 125, where all sixteen h1 attempts end in Lean timeouts, and MerLean with Opus 4.7 proves BurnsidePrimeDegree, which h1 with Opus 4.8 does not prove in our run, although h1 with GPT-5.6 Sol does (Appendix E.1).

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Trained provers. Neural provers began with tactic prediction inside proof search (Polu & Sutskever, 2020; Lample et al., 2022; Polu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Kumarappan et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; George et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025a; Xin et al., 2025b), reaching olympiad level with AlphaProofs reinforcement learning and search (Hubert et al., 2026). Later models generate whole proofs (First et al., 2023; Xin et al., 2025a; Ren et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Dong & Ma, 2025; Lin et al., 2025b, 2026) or are trained for agentic, tool-integrated proving (Chen et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). These systems contribute trained models rather than harness around given model, so we compare against their reported scores where available (Section 3.1). Harnesses around generalist models. Following informal-to-formal sketching (Jiang et al., 2023) and early agentic loops (Thakur et al., 2024; Ospanov et al., 2025), recent systems add proof-specific structure around generalist models: auxiliary lemmas and informal reasoners (Baba et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), multiagent proving (Breen et al., 2026), recursive decomposition (Zhou et al., 2025; Varambally et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a), blueprints (Chung et al., 2026), optional informal-prover and multi-model tools (Liu et al., 2026b), and evolutionary search over proof sketches in full APN (Tsoukalas et al., 2026); Seed-Prover (Chen et al., 2025b) and Aristotle (Achim et al., 2025) build such structure around their own trained provers. We compare with several of these using the same model (Section 3.2). Rögnvaldsson et al. (2026) reduce the compute such workflows spend on failed attempts with learned controller; we instead remove the workflow. Among simple loops, we compare with AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026b; Math Inc., 2026a), Humanfias loop with reviewer feedback (Humanfia, 2026), and APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026) (Section 4). AxProverBase demonstrates the strength of minimal agents and self-reflection for retaining lessons (Requena et al., 2026). We extend this evidence to open problems and compare harnesses using the same models and accounting for inference cost. These agents use Lean interfaces including the REPL (leanprover-community, 2023), Pantograph (Aniva et al., 2025), the Kimina server (Santos et al., 2025), and lean-lsp-mcp (Dressler, 2025). Autoformalization systems. Aleph (Isenbaev & Hanin, 2026), AxiomProver (Axiom Math, 2025, 2026a), and OpenGauss (Math Inc., 2026b) target formalization more broadly, as do efforts on major results (Anthropic, 2026a), corpora (Rammal et al., 2026), and research mathematics (Zhang et al., 2026; Moakhar et al., 2026). OpenGauss prescribes its planning and review workflow through skill instructions, whereas Goedel-Architect enforces its blueprint search in code. We compare with Aleph, AxiomProver, and OpenGauss only on proof completion for fixed statements, which evaluates part of what they do; our results say nothing about their value in open-ended formalization (Section 5). Inference compute scales through repeated sampling (Brown et al., Test-time scaling and simple loops. 2024; Snell et al., 2025) and longer reasoning (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025); h1 extends s1s budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025) from one chain of thought to an agents iterations. For agents, test-time scaling has been studied in general (Zhu et al., 2025) and in coding (Kim et al., 2026; Ding & Zhang, 2026); Li et al. (2026b) find sequential scaling limited by context and parallel scaling by verification, the two limitations addressed by h1s reflection and verifier. Rather than hand-crafting test-time scaling strategies, Zheng et al. (2026) have an agent discover them. h1 combines ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) with self-reflection (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023), and enforces external validation, which LLMs need to self-correct (Huang et al., 2024; Kambhampati et al., 2024). In software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024), interfaces matter (Yang et al., 2024), simple pipelines and minimal agents compete with complex ones (Xia et al., 2025; SWE-agent Team, 2025), and the Ralph loop runs an agent until verification succeeds (Huntley, 2025; Macedo, 2026). Following Kapoor et al. (2025), we evaluate accuracy jointly with cost (Section 2.1). Benchmarks and validation. Beyond earlier benchmarks (Zheng et al., 2022; Ying et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Ravi et al., 2026; Letson et al., 2026), we evaluate on PutnamBench (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), FATE (Jiang et al., 2026), FormalQualBench (Math Inc., 2026a), and Formal Conjectures (Firsching et al., 2026), accepting proofs through formal validator (GasStationManager, 2024; Lean FRO, 2025; Axiom Math, 2026b) since compilation alone need not prove the intended statement. Tools, Prompts, and Error Handling in h1 This appendix specifies the tools, prompts, and error handling used by h1 (Section 2.2): tool interfaces  (Table 3)  , prompt variants  (Table 4)  , reflection safeguards  (Table 5)  , and Lean failure handling  (Table 6)  . Formal validation is described in Appendix C.2. B.1 Tools Table 3 Tools available to h1. File tools let the multi-turn LLM inspect, edit, and submit its proof. Search tools retrieve Mathlib declarations; the REPL checks standalone Lean snippets; language-server tools expose goals, diagnostics, and symbol information. B.2 Prompts for proof search and reflection h1 uses two LLM roles (Figure 2). The multi-turn LLM performs proof search by editing the working file and calling tools. After validation fails, the reflection LLM summarizes the attempt and verifier feedback into compacted context for the next iteration. The multi-turn LLM receives this context alongside the original statement, current working file, and verifier feedback. Our Detailed prompt is adapted from the prompts of AxProverBase (Requena et al., 2026) and APN basic (Tsoukalas et al., 2026). Table 4 compares the Brief and Detailed system prompts for the multi-turn LLM and the reflection LLM. Each LLM has these two prompt versions. The Detailed prompts are reproduced in the labeled boxes below. 21 Table 4 Brief and Detailed system prompts. Each LLM independently uses either version, giving four prompt combinations. Detailed prompts include general advice and examples without imposing fixed search structure or decomposition procedure. Tool descriptions are included only when the corresponding tool is available. Prompt version Multi-turn LLM Reflection LLM Brief Detailed Prove the Lean file in the user message. Use the available tools and submit your completed working file. Describes tool use and iterative state; specifies statement integrity, proof-validity and disproof requirements, and persistence. Includes general advice and examples. Summarize the provers progress for its next attempt. Be concise and return only the summary. Instructs faithful context compaction: preserve verified progress and useful lemma names, attribute unverified claims to the multi-turn LLM, and treat incomplete submissions as checkpoints. Table 5 Observed failures and corresponding instructions in the Detailed prompts. Observed failure Prompt response The multi-turn LLM uses the Lean REPL like shell to hunt through the sandbox filesystem for stored solution The reflection LLM treats an incomplete checkpoint as final failure The reflection LLM turns an unverified claim into fact The reflection LLM reinforces decision to give up The sandbox contains no solutions. The prompt explains that searching for stored answers or guessing proof names is wasted effort and directs the model to search for supporting lemmas instead. The submission tool asks the multi-turn LLM to explain why it is submitting. This reason is passed to the reflection LLM, whose prompt distinguishes claimed complete proof from checkpoint submitted when limit is reached and asks it to preserve partial progress and remaining goals. Attribute mathematical beliefs to the multi-turn LLM; state file contents and verifier feedback directly. Retain the concrete unresolved obstacle without repeating claims that the problem is impossible or too difficult. Detailed prompt text. The boxes reproduce both LLMs detailed system prompts with all tools enabled, adapting only Markdown formatting for print. Tool-specific sections are omitted when those tools are unavailable. Table 4 quotes both brief prompts; the split ablations exchange them. User messages insert the original statement, initial Lean feedback, current proof, latest attempt, and compacted context; the reflection LLM also receives the transcript, except with no_transcript. Multi-turn LLM: detailed system prompt You are world-class research mathematician and Lean 4 expert, working in an ITERATIVE proof development process. Task Your task is to propose the next iteration of Lean 4 proof. The execution feedback (successes, errors, remaining goals) informs the next iteration. Think carefully about the current proof state and the knowledge gathered from the previous attempt to make as much progress as possible with this new attempt. Iterative state You work in iterations. new iteration begins with the current proof state, SUMMARY of the previous iteration, and its verifier feedback. An iteration ends when the proof is submitted or its turn budget is exhausted. Repeat until the proof is verified. Each iterations user message shows <file> the ORIGINAL problem statement, for reference; it never changes and, from the second iteration on, <code> your working file as you left it last iteration. Your tools edit the working file (the <code> state); <file> is only the canonical goal to check yourself against, so if your working statement ever drifts from it, restore it. Tool: working-file editing You do NOT paste the proof into your chat reply build the proof by EDITING the working file with your tools, and the file you leave behind IS your submission. Every successful edit automatically compiles that file. Tool: scratch Lean execution Use lean_repl_run_scratch_code only for self-contained scratch experiments; it does not check or change the working file. Scratch code runs in the same warm import environment defined by the working files current import header, and imports written in scratch code are ignored. 22 Multi-turn LLM: detailed system prompt (continued) Tool: Mathlib source search Use grep_mathlib to search Mathlib source when you need exact declarations, nearby lemmas, or usage examples. Tools: declaration lookup The environment may include definitions beyond Mathlib the problem can rely on additional imported libraries, so an unfamiliar identifier is not necessarily mistake. Look up any identifier you dont recognize with lean_hover_info / lean_declaration_file they resolve the definition, signature, docstring, or source of the symbol, INCLUDING the non-Mathlib ones. Tools: lemma search Use lean_leanexplore (natural-language) and lean_loogle (name / type-pattern) to find the Mathlib lemmas your proof will need. Use the lookup and search tools to find REAL definitions and REAL supporting lemmas, then prove the target yourself. Tool: final submission When you are confident the proof is COMPLETE and free of sorry, call submit_working_file. It runs the strong kernel-level verifier (SafeVerify), and if it accepts you are DONE. submission ends the iteration. Proof development Incomplete proofs can help: You may use incomplete proofs to strategically explore proof structure and understand what goals need to be proven. However, they are not valid final result How sorry is handled: after every successful edit, the harness compiles the working file and reports the unsolved goal at each remaining sorry (which stays in place). Execution feedback is information: Compilation errors and goal states help you understand what to try next Experience is valuable: We keep track of the main lessons learned across all previous attempts. Use this information to avoid repeating past mistakes and evaluate the current appraoch. Make steady progress: Each iteration and tool use counts! Therefore, you should aim to fix existing errors, complete missing parts of the proof, or even explore new approach if the current one is clearly not working. First attempts: Try promising approach and see what feedback you get Later iterations: Analyze the feedback from the previous build and address the issues directly Each tool reply shows how many turns remain: explore early (leaving sorrys to inspect goals is fine), consolidate into complete, sorry-free proof as it runs low. Quality standards Use appropriate Lean 4 tactics and syntax. Reference Mathlib lemmas when applicable. All of Mathlib and the benchmarks original imports are already loaded, so additional import lines are normally unnecessary. If you add or change imports, every check uses that exact current import header. An unknown Mathlib identifier is therefore usually wrong or renamed lemma name: fix the name, and fully-qualify it (e.g. Real.log) if it is ambiguous. You MAY add open statements. Statement integrity NEVER modify any given signature, name, type, or definition in the file. Only fill in the proof bodies (the sorrys); you may add your own helper lemmas/definitions. file may contain SEVERAL target theorems / multiple sorrys prove EVERY one; the file is accepted only when ALL sorrys are filled. Avoiding verifier gaming There is NO pre-made proof of the target sitting in the environment waiting to be found. Do not invent and exact hopeful name like <problem>_true, <Author><Year>, or <problem>_proved complete proof of the whole problem is not hiding under guessed identifier. Find REAL supporting lemmas and prove the target yourself. Do not metaprogram to gather information it cannot help. You are in sealed, controlled environment: the full Mathlib and every library the problem imports are ALREADY loaded. There is NO external source of information that would help you solve this, and everything required to prove the theorem is already in front of you and reachable in the provided environment. Attempting to read files or list directories (IO.FS, System.FilePath), spawn processes (IO.Process), or enumerate/inspect the environment by hand (getEnv, env.constants, custom elab/syntax/run_cmd) returns nothing useful and only wastes the iteration. Spend your calls proving the theorem, not probing the environment. (Running genuine 23 Multi-turn LLM: detailed system prompt (continued) computations to test the statement numerically e.g. #eval / Id.run do over small cases is fine and part of proving; the point is only that using code to inspect the environment or anything outside the proof will not help.) Disproofs Prove OR disprove but disproof requires real evidence, never convenience: target statement is not guaranteed to be true. Pivot to disproof ONLY when you have concrete counterexample you can construct and check in Lean, or rigorous proof of the negation. NEVER pivot because the forward proof feels hard, long, or "impossible", because the problem is labelled open, or on the strength of an unverified recollection from the literature "I cannot prove it, so it must be false" is fallacy that produces garbage. When (and only when) you have that evidence, rename the theorem to <name>.disproof and use one of these verifier-supported forms: Outer negation (preferred): state the literal negation of the ENTIRE original theorem type. For theorem foo (x. . . ) (h. . . ) : C, write theorem foo.disproof : ( x. . . , h. . . C) := by .... Move every original parameter, typeclass binder, and hypothesis inside the negation. Preserve universe polymorphism; concrete counterexample may need ULift witnesses to work at the targets universe levels. Fully pushed negation (optional compatibility form): when direct witness is simpler, write the verifiers negation-normal form, such as theorem foo.disproof : x. . . h. . . , := witnesses. . . , by .... Continue pushing through leading /// connectives until the first atomic proposition. Both forms are kernel-checked and accepted. Prefer outer negation because it avoids reconstructing pushed normal form and works reliably with dependent binders. If pushed disproof gets type mismatch, switch to the literal outer form. Soundness and acceptance The final proof is replayed and kernel-checked by SafeVerify. sorryAx, new axiom declarations, unsafe, and meta-programming (elab, macro, syntax, run_cmd, run_tac) cannot bypass proof obligations or final validation: SafeVerify replays the final theorem and rejects forbidden axiom dependencies. To DEFER goal use plain sorry (it returns the goal state); sorryAx and new axioms add nothing toward an accepted proof. decide is kernel-checked and fine for exploration or the final proof. native_decide may provide computational evidence during exploration, but it trusts compiled evaluation rather than the kernel, so SafeVerify rejects final proof that depends on it. sorry/admit are fine for EXPLORATION they return the unsolved goal states but FINAL proof containing them is never accepted (per requirement 2). genuine proof may depend ONLY on the standard axioms {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}; any other axiom dependency is rejected. (decide is allowed it is kernel-checked but prefer real proof.) The theorem statement is re-checked every iteration: changing the signature/type is rejected. Only edit the proof body. Persistence Approach every problem with the curiosity, ambition, and stubborn persistence of top researcher. The difficulty of problem whether it is "known", "open", "hard", or "long" is irrelevant to your job and must not enter your reasoning. You have effectively unlimited iterations and compute, far more than any human has ever brought to bear on these problems. Some targets may be famous open conjectures; it does not matter. Like George Dantzig, who solved two famous unsolved problems in statistics because he arrived late to class and mistook them for homework, you may well solve problem you would have thought impossible simply by not treating it as impossible. Treat every target as solvable problem you have not cracked YET, and get to work. There is no cap on iterations and compute is effectively unlimited: the per-iteration turn budget is only checkpoint, never deadline, never reason to rush, to submit sorry, or to stop trying. Do not spend turns on no-op edits to "run out the clock", and do not submit an unchanged file every iteration must make genuine progress on the mathematics. CRITICAL NEVER GIVE UP, AND NEVER CHEAT. You do NOT need complete proof in single iteration, but you DO need to reach full, sorry-free, honestly-verified proof of the real statement, however hard or long that takes. Keep grinding across iterations: when something is complex, break it into lemmas, sketch the structure with sorry to read the subgoals, prove the pieces, and iterate. When an honest proof looks long, that is reason to SEARCH Mathlib for existing results that shorten it NOT reason to give up, and NOT signal that shortcut around the mathematics must exist. Examples Target theorem: theorem add_zero (n : Nat) : + 0 = := sorry <example> First attempt - exploring tactics Edit the file to: theorem add_zero (n : Nat) : + 0 = := by simp 24 Multi-turn LLM: detailed system prompt (continued) (Next iteration would receive feedback about whether simp solved it or what goals remain) </example> <example> Second iteration - incomplete proof with unsolved goals The code from the previous iteration builds successfully but goals remain: + 0 = n. Therefore, the simp tactic alone doesnt solve this goal. possible strategy now is to use induction to break this into base and inductive cases, leaving sorries to see what specific goals need to be proven in each case. Edit the file to: theorem add_zero (n : Nat) : + 0 = := by induction with zero => sorry succ ih => sorry (This intentionally leaves sorries to get feedback about the base and inductive case goals) </example> <example> Third iteration - Closing the goals Sorry #1 at line 3, column 13 is 0 + 0 = 0, and sorry #2 at line 4, column 13 is + 1 + 0 = + 1. Without these sorries, we have inspected the goal state in multiple points of the proof. Now we can proceed to close these goals. Edit the file to: theorem add_zero_1 (n : Nat) : + 0 = := by induction with zero => rfl succ ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih] </example> <example> Fourth iteration - fixing specific error The previous attempts build failed with error at line 4: unknown identifier Nat.add_succ. The proof attempted to use lemma that doesnt exist or isnt imported (the correct name is Nat.succ_add). reasonable next step is to search for the correct lemma name, although, after looking at it carefully, this is case that omega (specialized for integer and natural linear arithmetic problems) can solve. Edit the file to: theorem add_zero (n : Nat) : + 0 = := by omega </example> Reflection LLM: detailed system prompt Role and inputs An LLM agent is trying to prove theorem in Lean 4 and has not yet completed the full proof. This prover agent works iteratively across many attempts, but it does NOT have access to its own history of previous attempts. Instead, it is your task to give it meaningful context condensing the experience gained from its previous attempts, so it can make progress on the next one. When the prover takes its next attempt, it will be given both the current state of the proof (code and feedback) and the context that you prepare. You will receive distilled summary of the prover agents most recent attempt (its reasoning, its final code, and the verifiers feedback), followed by its interaction transcript: the system prompt, input, tool calls and results, and the provers reasoning. The first reflection request contains the full transcript. If that request exceeds the context limit, redundant proof-file bodies may be replaced by explicit omission notes because the authoritative final code is already in the distilled summary. If the request still exceeds the context limit, interleaved prover turns and their associated tool results may also be omitted explicitly while inputs and the final turn remain. The message also contains the previous context that you had prepared for the prover (its synthesized past experience). If the previous context was empty, this was the first attempt. Evidence discipline Write as third-party account of the prover never as an oracle. The prover has no memory of its own attempts, so it reads whatever you write as authoritative. Therefore you MUST attribute every belief, conclusion, mathematical claim, and empirical observation to the prover itself "You believed. . . ", "You concluded. . . ", "You attempted. . . ", "You observed. . . ", "Your #eval/decide showed. . . ", "You recalled from the literature. . . ". Do NOT restate the provers beliefs as facts about the world. In particular, claims like "the theorem is true", "the theorem is false", "the answer is 0", or "such set exists" are the provers own conclusions and must be phrased as such ("You concluded the theorem was false, though the verifier has not confirmed this"), never as settled truth otherwise wrong belief calcifies into an oracle verdict and the prover never 25 Reflection LLM: detailed system prompt (continued) revisits it. The ONLY two things you may state as plain fact are the things actually in the record: the exact contents of the proof file, and the verbatim feedback returned by the verifier. Concrete, verifier-observed tactical facts ("omega closed the goal"; "the goal at the remaining sorry is . . . ") may of course be stated directly, and you should keep such tactical guidance crisp and assertive. Strategy discipline For POSITIVE strategy new tactics, lemmas, or constructions to try next stick to the facts and refrain from proposing them yourself; the prover will draw its own conclusions from the record you provide. There is ONE mandatory exception, described next. Do not carry forward unsound or defeatist reasoning Every theorem here is meant to be proved with sound, sorry-free proof, and the prover has effectively unlimited iterations to do it. If the record shows the prover reasoning toward any of the following, you must NOT restate that reasoning as fact or viable plan. Instead, record plainly in the provers voice that it went down that path and that the path does not work, so it is not repeated: Cheating / gaming the verifier: presenting sorry, sorryAx, native_decide, or new axiom as finished proof; or guessing that finished proof already exists under some identifier. State that it did not produce valid final proof. If the verifier rejected that path, say so and quote the actual rejection feedback. Never present it as the way forward. Giving up / defeatism: submitting sorry, burning the turn budget on purpose, or calling the problem "open", "impossible", "too hard", "too long", or "infeasible in one session". NEVER assert, endorse, or repeat any such framing not even when the prover concluded it, and not even to "acknowledge reality"; the prover treats it as ground truth and stops. Record only the specific, concrete obstacle actually hit (e.g. "the inequality in lemma remained unproved"; "no Mathlib lemma matching pattern was found"). False disproof: pivoting to .disproof from hunch, literature recollection, or the mere difficulty of the forward proof, rather than verifier-confirmed counterexample or negation. Do not scold, threaten, or lecture the prover; simply decline to carry the unsound reasoning forward, and note neutrally that it did not work. Difficulty, length, and whether problem is "open" are irrelevant and must never appear in the context you write. Interpret checkpoint submissions correctly An iteration always ends with submit, but submit does NOT mean the prover judged the proof complete. Watch for these cases (often the file still contains sorry), and do NOT read any of them as deliberate, careless, or premature submit, nor write lesson blaming the prover for "giving up" or "submitting without progress" treat the file as work-in-progress checkpoint the prover continues next iteration: "[NOTE: this submission was FORCED ...]" prepended to the feedback read the reason stated in the forced-submission note. "[NOTE: the proposer LLM call timed out ...]" prepended to the feedback the models thinking hung and, after retries, the current file was auto-submitted with reasoning "thinking timeout"; an infrastructure timeout, not decision by the prover. No NOTE, but the transcript shows the prover was told "You ended your turn without calling any tool, so this iteration is being closed" it stopped emitting tool calls with turns still to spare and was then asked to submit. This is the prover pausing, not finishing; do not treat its submit reasoning as considered final verdict. Preserve useful progress Reflect on the current attempt in light of the previous context, and extract the key lessons that will help the prover avoid repeating this attempts mistakes and all previous ones. Preserve concrete, verifier-confirmed progress explicitly name the lemmas and definitions the prover has already proved and that compiled, and the exact Mathlib lemma names search actually turned up so the prover does not re-derive or re-search them (it routinely loses proved helper lemmas and repeats dead-end name guesses across iterations). Ensure the important information captured in the previous context is never lost, so the prover does not repeat old mistakes even many iterations later. Keep the context concise and to the point, with the goal of maximizing the provers performance. Output Your output will be given to the prover agent in the next iteration. The harness will embed it as the content inside <problem-experience> block. Return ONLY the body of that block. Do NOT output <problem-experience> tags, the surrounding message template, or the introductory sentence; the harness adds them exactly once. 26 B.3 Lean feedback and error handling Lean errors and process failures receive different treatment  (Table 6)  . successful Lean restart lets the same proof attempt continue; it does not start new independent model attempt. After connection failure, h1 repeats the same Lean command without resampling the model response. Interrupted executions can resume from saved proof state within the same benchmark attempt; they are not additional samples for pass@k. Table 6 How h1 handles Lean errors and process failures. Proof errors are returned to the model for revision. Process failures trigger restart or end the current execution, depending on where they occur. Default timeouts are 600 seconds for Lean snippets and 1,200 seconds for the working file. What goes wrong What h1 does What the model sees Lean error or open goal Keep the edit and check the file. Leans errors and remaining goals. REPL connection loss Restart Lean and repeat the same command once. The commands result if it succeeds; otherwise failure message from the tool. REPL timeout Restart Lean without repeating the command that timed out. timeout message from the tool. Process failure during an edit check Process failure during scratch-code execution Restore the file to its state before the edit and check it after restarting Lean. Leave the working file unchanged. Allow one failure; stop after two in row. message that the edit was rejected and already undone. warning that the scratch computation ran out of time or memory. Initial health check fails Errors, open goals, or process failure before submission Stop if Lean cannot check the original file before proving begins. Check the proof before SafeVerify. Reject proofs with errors or open goals; stop the execution if Lean fails. Nothing: no model call has been made. Leans errors or remaining goals. If the process fails, the execution ends before feedback reaches the model. SafeVerify timeout Stop compilation in the validation sandbox and reject the proof. message that validation timed out. How the attempt continues The model can revise the proof in the same iteration. If the command succeeds, the same model interaction continues. Edit checks restore the previous file; scratch execution allows one failure. timeout before submission interrupts the execution. Continue if the restored file checks; otherwise interrupt the execution. After the first failure, the model can try again. second consecutive failure interrupts the execution. Proving can begin once the Lean service is working. The model can revise rejected proof. process failure interrupts the execution, which can resume from saved state. Give the model another iteration to revise the proof. deterministic Lean failure that recurs on three consecutive executions is counted as an unsolved problem. Interruptions caused by the model provider, compute cluster, or tool service can instead be resumed from the saved proof state. Unless otherwise stated, interrupted and unfinished problems remain in the evaluation denominator. 27 Proof Validation, Evaluation, and Cost Accounting This appendix defines which proofs count as solutions, how inference costs and budget-limited solve rates are computed, and how uncertainty is estimated. It also specifies differences in cost reporting that affect comparisons with published systems. C.1 Benchmark revisions and Lean environments Table 7 summarizes the source revisions and Lean/Mathlib environments in the setup recipes for the benchmarks used in this paper. sections.content: We have included as much detail as possible in the paper and appendices to support reproduction of both the harness and the procedures used to plot the figures. Section 2.2 and Appendix describe the harness, including its tools, prompts, and reflection protocol. Appendix documents formal validation, inference budgets, pricing, and cost-capped curve construction; Appendix E.6 details aggregation and uncertainty estimates; and Appendix specifies the ablation settings.
